Pareto-Optimal Offline Reinforcement Learning via Smooth Tchebysheff Scalarization

Aadyot Bhatnagar ††thanks: Profluent Bio, Inc.††thanks: To whom correspondence should be addressed: {abhatnagar,ali}@profluent.bio    Peter Mørch Groth11footnotemark: 1    Ali Madani11footnotemark: 1 22footnotemark: 2
Abstract

Large language models can be aligned with human preferences through offline reinforcement learning (RL) on small labeled datasets. While single-objective alignment is well-studied, many real-world applications demand the simultaneous optimization of multiple conflicting rewards, e.g. optimizing both catalytic activity and specificity in protein engineering, or helpfulness and harmlessness for chatbots. Prior work has largely relied on linear reward scalarization, but this approach provably fails to recover non-convex regions of the Pareto front. In this paper, instead of scalarizing the rewards directly, we frame multi-objective RL itself as an optimization problem to be scalarized via smooth Tchebysheff scalarization, a recent technique that overcomes the shortcomings of linear scalarization. We use this formulation to derive Smooth Tchebysheff Optimization of Multi-Objective Preferences (STOMP), a novel offline RL algorithm that extends direct preference optimization to the multi-objective setting in a principled way by standardizing the individual rewards based on their observed distributions. We empirically validate STOMP on a range of protein engineering tasks by aligning three autoregressive protein language models on three laboratory datasets of protein fitness. Compared to state-of-the-art baselines, STOMP achieves the highest hypervolumes in eight of nine settings according to both offline off-policy and generative evaluations. We thus demonstrate that STOMP is a powerful, robust multi-objective alignment algorithm that can meaningfully improve post-trained models for multi-attribute protein optimization and beyond.

1 Introduction

Large language models have been trained on massive corpora of text, code, images, and proteins [79, 46, 50, 12, 18, 63, 19]. These models are powerful density estimators for the data distributions they were trained on, but they often require supervised post-training via algorithms like reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to align their likelihoods with the preferences of their users [58, 91, 16]. RL-based alignment is an incredibly general paradigm that has been used to train chatbots [58, 4, 64], improve text-to-image generators [41, 39], and enable protein language models to generate proteins with higher fitness [7, 35, 81, 82].

While single-objective RL is well-studied, many real-world applications demand the simultaneous optimization of multiple conflicting objectives. For example, chatbots should be helpful to their users, but their responses should also be safe [4]. Text-to-image models should generate images that are both high-quality and aligned with their prompts [39]. Protein engineers may seek a protein with both high activity and specificity [80, 22], or a highly active protein that maintains adequate stability and expression [2, 81]. Since no single solution can in general optimize all these rewards simultaneously, our goal is instead the Pareto front, i.e. the set of all non-dominated solutions.

Scalarizing the reward vector is a common approach to multi-objective RL, with linear scalarization (i.e. taking a weighted average) being the simplest strategy [40, 89, 81, 14, 86]. Unfortunately, linear reward scalarization is provably incapable of recovering solutions from non-convex regions of the Pareto front, and solutions from these regions often represent the exact compromises between conflicting objectives that we are the most interested in discovering [17, 10, 20, 78].

Lin et al. [42] introduce smooth Tchebysheff scalarization (STS) to address the shortcomings of linear scalarization. STS enjoys efficient gradient-based optimization and is able to find all solutions on the Pareto front. However, STS can be challenging to use off-the-shelf for reward scalarization because it is highly sensitive to the scales of the individual rewards due to its logsumexp formulation.

In this work, rather than using STS to scalarize the rewards directly, we observe that multi-objective RL is itself a multi-objective optimization problem that can be scalarized. We thus apply STS to the multi-objective RL problem and use this framing to derive smooth Tchebysheff reward scalarization. Crucially, smooth Tchebysheff reward scalarization dynamically standardizes the individual rewards based on their observed distributions in an offline training set, circumventing the per-reward scaling hyperparameters that would arise from a less principled application of STS.

Building on these insights, we introduce Smooth Tchebysheff Optimization of Multi-Objective Preferences (STOMP). STOMP is an offline RL algorithm that extends direct preference optimization [64] to align a language model’s likelihoods using an offline dataset that associates each sequence to multiple scalar-valued rewards. We empirically validate STOMP on a range of protein engineering tasks by aligning three autoregressive protein language models on three laboratory datasets of protein fitness. Across both offline off-policy and generative evaluations, we find that in eight of nine evaluation settings, STOMP achieves (or ties for) the highest hypervolumes compared to state-of-the-art baselines that use either linear scalarization or a more naive implementation of STS [49].

2 Preliminaries and Related Work

2.1 Reinforcement Learning

Given context x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, a language model or policy π\pi predicts the conditional probability π⁡(y|x)\pi(y|x) of sequences y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y}. Most reinforcement learning (RL) formulations for language models optimize the expected reward of sequences generated from π\pi while simultaneously requiring that π\pi does not deviate too much from a reference π0\pi_{0}, i.e. their KL divergence is less than η\eta. π0\pi_{0} is typically pre-trained or fine-tuned language model that we are further training with RL [68, 69, 16, 91]. Concretely, given a distribution over contexts 𝒫\mathcal{P} and a reward function r:𝒳×𝒴→ℝr:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R}, we seek to solve

argmaxπ𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)] s.t. 𝔻KL(π∣∣π0)≤η\displaystyle\argmax_{\pi}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}[r(x,y)]\text{\quad s.t. \quad}\mathbb{D}_{KL}(\pi\mid\mid\pi_{0})\leq\eta
=\displaystyle= argmaxπ𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[r(x,y)]−β𝔻KL(π∣∣π0)\displaystyle\argmax_{\pi}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}[r(x,y)]-\beta\mathbb{D}_{KL}(\pi\mid\mid\pi_{0})
=\displaystyle= argminπ𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)​[β​log⁡π⁡(y|x)−β​log⁡π0​(y|x)−r⁡(x,y)]\displaystyle\argmin_{\pi}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\beta\log\pi(y|x)-\beta\log\pi_{0}(y|x)-r(x,y)\right]
=\displaystyle= argminπ𝔻KL(π∣∣π⋆)\displaystyle\argmin_{\pi}\mathbb{D}_{KL}(\pi\mid\mid\pi^{\star})

Faury et al. [23, Lemma 5] prove that the optimal Lagrange multiplier is β=𝕍π0​[r⁡(x,y)]/2​η\beta=\sqrt{\mathbb{V}_{\pi_{0}}[r(x,y)]/2\eta}. Meanwhile, π⋆\pi^{\star} is the optimal policy and Z⁡(x)Z(x) is its partition function:

π⋆​(y|x)=1Z⁡(x)​π0​(y|x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)andZ⁡(x)=∑y∈𝒴π0​(y|x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)\displaystyle\pi^{\star}(y|x)=\frac{1}{Z(x)}\pi_{0}(y|x)\exp\left(r(x,y)/\beta\right)\quad\text{and}\quad Z(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\pi_{0}(y|x)\exp\left(r(x,y)/\beta\right)

Maximum-entropy reinforcement learning (MaxEntRL) is a special case that uses a uniform reference policy π0​(y|x)∝1\pi_{0}(y|x)\propto 1 [76, 90]. MaxEntRL favors more stochastic policies with more diverse generations, and it has certain distributional robustness guarantees [21].

2.2 Offline Reinforcement Learning via Preference Optimization

RL is challenging because it requires us to optimize the expected reward as sampled from the policy π\pi we are training. Direct preference optimization (DPO) [64] solves r⁡(x,y)=β​log⁡(π⋆​(y|x)/π0​(y|x))+β​log⁡Z⁡(x)r(x,y)=\beta\log(\pi^{\star}(y|x)/\pi_{0}(y|x))+\beta\log Z(x) and assumes the Bradley-Terry model [11] p⁡(y1≻y2|x)=σ⁡(r⁡(x,y1)−r⁡(x,y2))p(y_{1}\succ y_{2}|x)=\sigma(r(x,y_{1})-r(x,y_{2})) to recast this challenging RL problem as the more tractable maximum likelihood estimation problem of minimizing the following loss on an offline dataset:

ℒDPO(π;β,δ)=∑x,yw,ylr⁡(x,yw)>r⁡(x,yl)+δ−logσ(βlogπ⁡(yw|x)π0​(yw|x)−βlogπ⁡(yl|x)π0​(yl|x))\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DPO}}(\pi;\beta,\delta)=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y_{w},y_{l}\\ r(x,y_{w})>r(x,y_{l})+\delta\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!-\log\sigma\left(\beta\log\frac{\pi(y_{w}|x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{w}|x)}-\beta\log\frac{\pi(y_{l}|x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{l}|x)}\right) (1)

Here, ywy_{w} is a “winner” and yly_{l} is a “loser” according to the reward rr, while δ\delta ensures that we only compare samples with a sufficiently large reward difference. SimPO uses a uniform reference π0​(y|x)∝1\pi_{0}(y|x)\propto 1 and can be considered an instantiation of MaxEntRL in the DPO framework [51, 84].

Recent works enhance DPO by explicitly incorporating the reward difference r⁡(x,yw)−r⁡(x,yl)r(x,y_{w})-r(x,y_{l}) as a margin into similar paired losses [14, 27, 48, 24, 1, 81]. These methods leverage the difference

β​log⁡π⁡(yw|x)π⁡(yl|x)−β​log⁡π⋆​(yw|x)π⋆​(yl|x)\displaystyle\beta\log\frac{\pi(y_{w}|x)}{\pi(y_{l}|x)}\!-\!\beta\log\frac{\pi^{\star}(y_{w}|x)}{\pi^{\star}(y_{l}|x)} =(β​log⁡π⁡(yw|x)π0​(yw|x)−r⁡(x,yw)⏟Sπ​(x,yw,β))−(β​log⁡π⁡(yl|x)π0​(yl|x)−r⁡(x,yl)⏟Sπ​(x,yl,β))\displaystyle=\Big(\!\underbrace{\beta\log\frac{\pi(y_{w}|x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{w}|x)}\!-r(x,y_{w})}_{S^{\pi}(x,y_{w};\beta)}\!\Big)\!-\!\Big(\!\underbrace{\beta\log\frac{\pi(y_{l}|x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{l}|x)}\!-r(x,y_{l})}_{S^{\pi}(x,y_{l};\beta)}\!\Big)

to match the learned policy π\pi to the optimal policy π⋆\pi^{\star} and can be theoretically grounded in various ways. For example, squared loss methods [27, 24, 48] minimize (Sπ​(x,yw,β)−Sπ​(x,yl,β)+δ)2(S^{\pi}(x,y_{w};\beta)-S^{\pi}(x,y_{l};\beta)+\delta)^{2}, while OffsetDPO [1] minimizes

ℒODPO(π;β,δ)=∑x,yw,ylr⁡(x,yw)>r⁡(x,yl)+δ−logσ(Sπ(x,yw;β)−Sπ(x,yl;β)+δ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ODPO}}(\pi;\beta,\delta)=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y_{w},y_{l}\\ r(x,y_{w})>r(x,y_{l})+\delta\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!-\log\sigma\left(S^{\pi}(x,y_{w};\beta)-S^{\pi}(x,y_{l};\beta)+\delta\right) (2)

2.3 Multi-Objective Optimization

Multi-objective optimization seeks to minimize kk different losses 𝑳=L1,…,Lk\boldsymbol{L}=L_{1},\ldots,L_{k} simultaneously. Often, these losses will conflict with each other and cannot be simultaneously optimized by a single solution. We instead say that 𝑳⁡(z′)≺𝑳⁡(z)\boldsymbol{L}(z^{\prime})\prec\boldsymbol{L}(z) (i.e. z′z^{\prime} Pareto-dominates zz) if Li​(z′)≤Li​(z)L_{i}(z^{\prime})\leq L_{i}(z) for all ii and Li​(z′)<Li​(z)L_{i}(z^{\prime})<L_{i}(z) for at least one ii. The Pareto front of optimal solutions is the set of non-dominated solutions, i.e. {z∈𝒵:𝑳⁡(z′)⊀𝑳⁡(z)​∀z′∈𝒵}\{z\in\mathcal{Z}:\boldsymbol{L}(z^{\prime})\not\prec\boldsymbol{L}(z)\ \forall\ z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}\} [53].

Scalarization is a common approach to multi-objective optimization, with linear scalarization being the simplest strategy, i.e. min⁡∑i=1kz⁡λi​Li​(z)\min_{z}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}L_{i}(z) for some user-specified preference vector λ∈Δk−1\lambda\in\Delta^{k-1} on the simplex [53, 28]. Without loss of generality, we assume λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 for all ii. However, linear scalarization will fail to find any solutions from non-convex regions of the Pareto front [10, 17, 20].

Tchebysheff scalarization (TS) defines Li⋆=minz⁡Li​(z)L_{i}^{\star}=\min_{z}L_{i}(z) and optimizes minz⁡maxi​λi​(Li​(z)−Li⋆)\min_{z}\max_{i}\lambda_{i}(L_{i}(z)-L_{i}^{\star}). Under mild assumptions, it can find all solutions on the Pareto front by varying the preference vector λ\lambda [9, 72, 15]. However, the min-max formulation is non-differentiable and can be challenging to optimize in practice [29]. Lin et al. [42] introduce smooth Tchebysheff scalarization (STS), which instead optimizes minz⁡τ​log​∑i=1kexp⁡(λi​(Li​(z)−Li⋆)/τ)\min_{z}\tau\log\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp(\lambda_{i}(L_{i}(z)-L_{i}^{\star})/\tau). Here, τ\tau is a smoothing parameter, and STS approaches TS as τ→0+\tau\to 0^{+}. STS has many of the same favorable properties as classical TS while being more amenable to gradient-based optimization due to its smoothness.

3 Multi-Objective Offline Reinforcement Learning

In multi-objective (KL-constrained or MaxEnt) RL, we wish to simultaneously optimize kk reward functions r1,…,rkr_{1},\ldots,r_{k}. Letting η=1/(2​γ2)\eta=1/(2\gamma^{2}), this is equivalent to the multi-objective optimization

argmaxπ𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[ri(x,y)]i=1k s.t. 𝔻KL(π∣∣π0)≤12​γ2\displaystyle\argmax_{\pi}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[r_{i}(x,y)\right]_{i=1}^{k}\text{\quad s.t. \quad}\mathbb{D}_{KL}(\pi\mid\mid\pi_{0})\leq\frac{1}{2\gamma^{2}} (3)
=\displaystyle= argminπ𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)​[log⁡π⁡(y|x)−log⁡πi⋆​(y|x)]i=1k\displaystyle\argmin_{\pi}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\log\pi(y|x)-\log\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)\right]_{i=1}^{k} (4)
πi⋆​(y|x)=\displaystyle\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)= 1Zi​(x)​π0​(y|x)​exp⁡(ri​(x,y)γ​𝕍π0​[ri​(x,y)])\displaystyle\frac{1}{Z_{i}(x)}\pi_{0}(y|x)\exp\left(\frac{r_{i}(x,y)}{\gamma\sqrt{\mathbb{V}_{\pi_{0}}[r_{i}(x,y)]}}\right) (5)

In practice, we estimate σi2=𝕍π0​[ri​(x,y)]\sigma_{i}^{2}=\mathbb{V}_{\pi_{0}}[r_{i}(x,y)] as the empirical variance of ri​(x,y)r_{i}(x,y) on the full training set, hierarchically averaged over contexts x∼𝒫x\sim\mathcal{P}. Most recent multi-objective RL work linearly scalarizes the reward to reduce the problem to single-objective RL [40, 89, 81, 14, 86, 75]. It is straightforward to show that this is equivalent to linearly scalarizing Optimization Problem 4. Others consider alternative reward scalarizations, but they do not directly correspond to alternative scalarizations of Optimization Problem 4 [78, 83, 66, 32, 49].

3.1 Smooth Tchebysheff Reward Scalarization

We innovate on prior work by applying smooth Tchebysheff scalarization (STS) [42] directly to Optimization Problem 4. Our goal is to derive a scalarized reward RR with the property that an RR-optimal policy simultaneously minimizes an upper bound on its KL divergence from multiple optimal policies π1⋆,…,πk⋆\pi_{1}^{\star},\ldots,\pi_{k}^{\star}, one for each reward r1,…,rkr_{1},\ldots,r_{k}:

minπ⁡τ​log​∑i=1kexp⁡(λiτ​𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[log⁡π⁡(y|x)−log⁡πi⋆​(y|x)])\displaystyle\min_{\pi}\tau\log\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp\bigg(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\tau}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\log\pi(y|x)-\log\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)\right]\bigg)
≤\displaystyle\leq minπ⁡𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[τ​log​∑i=1kexp⁡(λiτ​(log⁡π⁡(y|x)−log⁡πi⋆​(y|x)))]\displaystyle\min_{\pi}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\tau\log\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\tau}(\log\pi(y|x)-\log\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x))\right)\right]
=\displaystyle= minπ⁡λmin​𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[log⁡π⁡(y|x)−τλmin​log⁡(∑i=1kπ​(y|x)(λi−λmin)/τπi⋆​(y|x)λi/τ)−1]\displaystyle\min_{\pi}\lambda_{\min}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\log\pi(y|x)-\frac{\tau}{\lambda_{\min}}\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\pi(y|x)^{(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{\min})/\tau}}{\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)^{\lambda_{i}/\tau}}\right)^{-1}\right] (6)
≤\displaystyle\leq minπ⁡λmin​𝔼x∼𝒫y∼π(⋅∣x)[log⁡π⁡(y|x)−τλmin​log⁡(∑i=1k1πi⋆​(y|x)λi/τ)−1]\displaystyle\min_{\pi}\lambda_{\min}\E_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim\mathcal{P}\\ y\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x)\end{subarray}}\left[\log\pi(y|x)-\frac{\tau}{\lambda_{\min}}\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{1}{\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)^{\lambda_{i}/\tau}}\right)^{-1}\right] (7)

The first upper bound is due to Jensen’s inequality, while the second follows from the fact that π​(y|x)(λi−λmin)/τ≤1\pi(y|x)^{(\lambda_{i}-\lambda_{\min})/\tau}\leq 1, with equality when λ1=⋯=λk=1/k\lambda_{1}=\cdots=\lambda_{k}=1/k. To avoid problematic dependencies between the scalarized reward and a potentially sub-optimal reference π0\pi_{0}, we let πi⋆​(y|x)∝exp⁡(ri​(x,y)/(γ​σi))\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)\propto\exp(r_{i}(x,y)/(\gamma\sigma_{i})) be the optimal policy under MaxEntRL.11 1 We also ran initial experiments with a variant of this reward scalarization derived from KL-constrained RL, i.e. πi⋆​(y|x)∝π0​(y|x)​exp⁡(ri​(x,y)/(γ​σi))\pi_{i}^{\star}(y|x)\propto\pi_{0}(y|x)\exp(r_{i}(x,y)/(\gamma\sigma_{i})). It significantly underperformed the MaxEntRL reward scalarization in the main text that is π0\pi_{0}-independent, primarily due to π0\pi_{0}’s influence on the partition functions Zi​(x)Z_{i}(x). Then, Optimization Problem 6 is a KL divergence minimization that is equivalent to performing MaxEntRL with reward

RSTλ,π(x,y;γ)=−γ​τλminlog∑i=1kexp(λi−λminτlogπ(y|x)−λiτ(ri​(x,y)γ​σi−logZi(x)))\displaystyle R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi}(x,y;\gamma)\!=-\frac{\gamma\tau}{\lambda_{\min}}\!\log\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda_{i}\!-\!\lambda_{\min}}{\tau}\log\pi(y|x)-\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\tau}\bigg(\frac{r_{i}(x,y)}{\gamma\sigma_{i}}-\log Z_{i}(x)\bigg)\!\right) (8)

RSTλ(x,y;γ)=−γ​τλminlog∑i=1kexp(−λiτ(ri​(x,y)γ​σi−logZi(x)))\displaystyle R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda}(x,y;\gamma)=-\frac{\gamma\tau}{\lambda_{\min}}\log\sum_{i=1}^{k}\exp\left(-\frac{\lambda_{i}}{\tau}\bigg(\frac{r_{i}(x,y)}{\gamma\sigma_{i}}-\log Z_{i}(x)\bigg)\right) (9)

The policy-independent RSTλR_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda} is useful in settings where the dependency of RSTλ,πR_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi} on the training policy π\pi could cause instability. In practice, we use the training set {(xm,ym(n)):m∈[M],n∈[Nm]}\{(x_{m},y_{m}^{(n)}):m\in[M],n\in[N_{m}]\} to estimate the intractable partition functions Zi​(x)Z_{i}(x):

log⁡Z^i​(xm)\displaystyle\log\hat{Z}_{i}(x_{m}) =log∑n=1Nmexp(ri​(xm,ym(n))γ​σi)\displaystyle=\log\sum_{n=1}^{N_{m}}\exp\bigg(\frac{r_{i}(x_{m},y_{m}^{(n)})}{\gamma\sigma_{i}}\bigg)

This estimator ensures that the distribution-relative reward ρi​(x,y)=ri​(x,y)/σi−γ​log⁡Z^i​(x)≤0\rho_{i}(x,y)=r_{i}(x,y)/\sigma_{i}-\gamma\log\hat{Z}_{i}(x)\leq 0 uniformly. This condition is required for reward scalarization 9 to cover the full Pareto front [42].

To build intuition for Equation 9, we first note that limτ→0+λmin​RSTλ​(x,y,γ)=mini⁡λi​ρi​(x,y)\lim_{\tau\to 0^{+}}\lambda_{\min}R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda}(x,y;\gamma)=\min_{i}\lambda_{i}\rho_{i}(x,y). In other words, as τ→0+\tau\to 0^{+}, sequences yy with high RSTλ​(x,y,γ)R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda}(x,y;\gamma) must simultaneously have high distribution-relative rewards ρi​(x,y)\rho_{i}(x,y) for all ii. With this in mind, we visualize different standardizations for four rewards in Figure 1. Rewards r1−2r_{1-2} are left-skewed, while r3−4r_{3-4} are right-skewed.

Because more sequences have high r3−4r_{3-4} than r1−2r_{1-2}, a good standardization should penalize the rare sequences with low r3−4r_{3-4} more aggressively than the common sequences with low r1−2r_{1-2}. Conversely, it should favor high r1−2r_{1-2} more than it favors high r3−4r_{3-4}. Min-max standardization (Column 1) does the opposite. Mean-variance standardization (Column 2) achieves this goal to some extent, but the effect is limited by design and over-indexes on outliers. The partition functions ZiZ_{i} allow the distribution-relative rewards ρi\rho_{i} (Column 3) to favor high r1−2r_{1-2} more than high r3−4r_{3-4} without placing as much weight on outliers as mean-variance standardization. Now, let

λ¯i∝(1M∑m=1M1Nm∑n=1Nm−ρi(xm,ym(n)))−1\displaystyle\bar{\lambda}_{i}\propto\left(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{1}{N_{m}}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{m}}-\rho_{i}(x_{m},y_{m}^{(n)})\right)^{-1} (10)

be the preference vector that re-weights the ρi\rho_{i}’s to all have the same mean. λ¯i​ρi​(x,y)\bar{\lambda}_{i}\rho_{i}(x,y) (Column 4) compresses left-skewed rewards r1−2r_{1-2} and stretches right-skewed r3−4r_{3-4} to penalize the rare sequences with low r3−4r_{3-4} more than the common sequences with low r1−2r_{1-2}. r4r_{4} is more right-skewed than r3r_{3}, so this effect is even more pronounced. Different preferences λ\lambda achieve different tradeoffs.

3.2 Smooth Tchebysheff Optimization of Multi-Objective Preferences (STOMP)

To design a practical offline multi-objective RL algorithm, we define the difference

DSTλ,π​(x,yw,yl,β,γ)\displaystyle\!\!D_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi}(x,y_{w},y_{l};\beta,\gamma) =β⁡(log⁡π⁡(yw|x)π0​(yw|x)−log⁡π⁡(yl|x)π0​(yl|x))−(RSTλ,π​(x,yw,γ)−RSTλ,π​(x,yl,γ))\displaystyle=\beta\bigg(\!\!\log\frac{\pi(y_{w}|x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{w}|x)}\!-\!\log\frac{\pi(y_{l}|x)}{\pi_{0}(y_{l}|x)}\!\bigg)\!-\!\left(\!R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi}(x,y_{w};\gamma)\!-\!R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi}(x,y_{l};\gamma)\right) (11)

We then adapt OffsetDPO [1] (Equation 2) to get the Smooth Tchebysheff Optimization of Multi-Objective Preferences (STOMP) loss

ℒSTOMP(π;α,β,γ,δ,λ)=∑x,yw,ylRSTλ​(x,yw,γ)>RSTλ​(x,yl,γ)+δ−logσ(DSTλ,π(x,yw,yl;β,γ)+δ)−α|yw|logπ(yw|x)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{STOMP{}}}(\pi;\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\delta,\lambda)=\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}x,y_{w},y_{l}\\ R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda}(x,y_{w};\gamma)>R_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda}(x,y_{l};\gamma)+\delta\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!-\log\sigma\Big(D_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi}(x,y_{w},y_{l};\beta,\gamma)+\delta\Big)-\frac{\alpha}{|y_{w}|}\log\pi(y_{w}|x) (12)

Notably, we use the policy-independent approximate reward RSTλR_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda} (Equation 9) to determine preference pairs, since having preferences evolve with the policy π\pi during training led to instability in early experiments. However, we use the policy-dependent reward RSTλ,πR_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi} (Equation 8) in the individual loss terms because it arises from a tighter bound to the optimization problem we are solving.

We also include the length-averaged negative log likelihood of the winners in each comparison, multiplied by a regularization coefficient α\alpha [60]. This regularization is especially important when the training dataset is not sampled from the reference policy π0\pi_{0}, a common reality in offline RL [26, 43]. It can also be practically helpful because DPO-style algorithms only increase the likelihood ratio of winners to losers, but they do not prevent the absolute likelihoods from degrading [7].

4 Experiments

We use preference optimization algorithms to align protein language models (PLMs) on laboratory data measuring a variety of biological attributes. We apply all methods to the autoregressive PLM ProGen3-3B (PG3) [7] and two internal retrieval-augmented PLMs similar to PoET [77]: ProGen-RA-3B (RA-3B) and ProGen-RA-10B (RA-10B), which have 3B and 10B parameters respectively.

While much of the PLM literature has focused on evaluating the correlation between a protein’s biological attributes and the likelihood a PLM assigns it [56, 50, 57, 87, 7, 73, 82, 55], this approach is inappropriate for multi-objective optimization where individual attributes may be uncorrelated or even anti-correlated. Instead, we turn to the problem statement of RL and estimate the expected rewards of sequences sampled from the PLM. We rely on the hypervolume enclosed by the non-dominated solutions of the expected rewards as our primary performance indicator [3, 85].

4.1 Datasets

DHFR

Romanowicz et al. [67] measure the activity of over 1500 diverse dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) homologs in the presence of varying concentrations of trimethoprim (TMP, a DHFR inhibitor). They express each protein using two codon optimizations. To reduce noise, we only consider proteins with at least 5 pruned barcode reads, we drop all missing values, and we average the activity across codon optimizations for each experimental setting. We hold out 139 random homologs as test data, and train on the remaining 310 homologs. We aim to maximize DHFR activity, both in the absence of TMP and in the presence of 50µg/mL of TMP (a high concentration that abolishes the activity of most DHFRs). These two objectives are uncorrelated (Spearman ρ=−0.010\rho=-0.010).

PbrR

PbrR is a Pb2+-specific binding protein that also exhibits non-specific binding for other divalent ions including Zn2+ [8, 37]. Wang et al. [80] perform active learning guided directed evolution to engineer PbrR to maximize the log2\log_{2}-fold change increase in Pb2+ binding and the log2\log_{2}-fold change decrease in Zn2+ binding. We seek to maximize the same two negatively correlated objectives (Spearman ρ=−0.806\rho=-0.806). We use as our training set their initial library consisting of 1076 single-mutation variants and 79 variants with 2–5 mutations from the wild type. Our test set consists of the 869 variants (with up to 12 mutations) that they designed over three rounds of engineering.

α-Amylase

The Align Foundation’s 2023 Protein Engineering Tournament introduced open source datasets for a wide range of proteins [2]. We use their dataset of α-amylase variants, which consists of 8076 single-mutation variants and 1879 variants with 4–10 mutations from the wild type. All proteins were assayed for activity, expression, and thermostability. Similar to the PbrR dataset, we aim to maximize all three properties simultaneously by training on the single-mutation variants and testing on the multi-mutation variants. The objectives are positively correlated, with activity/expression, activity/stability, and expression/stability respectively having Spearman ρ=0.655,0.602,0.719\rho=0.655,0.602,0.719.

4.2 Methods

As baselines, we test direct preference optimization (DPO [64], Equation 1) and OffsetDPO (ODPO [1], Equation 2) using the linear reward scalarization RLinλ​(x,y)=∑i=1kλi​ri​(x,y)/σiR_{\mathrm{Lin}}^{\lambda}(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}r_{i}(x,y)/\sigma_{i}. We refer to these methods as DPO-Lin and ODPO-Lin. We also evaluate ODPO-STZ, i.e. ODPO with the smooth Tchebysheff-like z-score (STZ) scalarization proposed by McCarter et al. [49]:

RSTZλ(x,y)=−log∑i=1kλiexp(−ri​(x,y)−μiσi)\displaystyle R_{\text{STZ}}^{\lambda}(x,y)=-\log\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\exp\left(-\frac{r_{i}(x,y)-\mu_{i}}{\sigma_{i}}\right)

Finally, we evaluate our method STOMP (Equation 12). The primary differences between ODPO-STZ and STOMP stem from the reward scalarization. ODPO-STZ centers each reward ri/σir_{i}/\sigma_{i} at its mean before taking the logsumexp, while STOMP centers at Zi​(x)Z_{i}(x). Figure 1 describes the benefits of our approach. ODPO-STZ also weights by λ\lambda outside the exponent to account for negative z-scores, while STOMP avoids this issue and follows the more principled approach of Lin et al. [42], weighting by λ\lambda inside the exponent to better navigate tradeoffs between different objectives.

Similar to Bhatnagar et al. [7], we just use the <bos> token as the context xx for PG3. However, for the RA models, we follow PoET’s prompt construction strategy [77] to construct 24 prompts x1,…,x24x_{1},\ldots,x_{24} with up to 4096 tokens of homologs discovered via ColabFold search [71, 54]. For the more diverse DHFR dataset, we use homologs >30% ID to any training sequence, while for the local mutational landscapes of PbrR and α-amylase, we use homologs >70% ID to the wild type.

For each (dataset, base model) pair, we train all algorithms with a range of preference vectors λ\lambda to probe how well each method can cover the full Pareto front. For PbrR, we train all models with each of λ∈{(13,23),(12,12),(23,13)}\lambda\in\left\{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}),(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}),(\frac{2}{3},\frac{1}{3})\right\}. For DHFR, we train with λ=(12,12)\lambda=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}). For α-amylase, we train with each of λ∈{(13,13,13),(14,14,12),(25,15,25)}\lambda\in\left\{(\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{3}),(\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2}),(\frac{2}{5},\frac{1}{5},\frac{2}{5})\right\} ordered as (activity, expression, stability).22 2 For our method STOMP, we actually train with the preference vector λi′=λi​λ¯i/∑i=1kλi​λ¯i\lambda_{i}^{\prime}=\lambda_{i}\bar{\lambda}_{i}/\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}\bar{\lambda}_{i}. Recall that λ¯\bar{\lambda} (Equation 10) re-weights the individual distribution-relative rewards to have the same mean. Thus, the transformation λ↦λ′\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{\prime} simply keeps the preference vector interpretable for STOMP. Across the different base models, datasets, preference vectors, and preference optimization algorithms, we train a total of 84 models. All other training hyperparameters are reported in Appendix B.

4.3 Offline Off-Policy Evaluations

In offline RL problems where we have access to a test set but cannot easily evaluate generations from the trained policy π\pi, accurately estimating the expected reward 𝔼π[ri​(x,y)]\E_{\pi}[r_{i}(x,y)] is a common challenge. A standard approach assumes that the test set is sampled from the reference policy π0\pi_{0} and uses importance sampling to estimate 𝔼π0[ri​(x,y)​π​(y|x)/π0​(y|x)]=𝔼π[ri​(x,y)]\E_{\pi_{0}}[r_{i}(x,y)\pi(y|x)/\pi_{0}(y|x)]=\E_{\pi}[r_{i}(x,y)]. However, because the propensity score π⁡(y|x)/π0​(y|x)\pi(y|x)/\pi_{0}(y|x) has high variance, we instead use the biased weighted importance sampling estimator on the test set {(xm,ym(n)):m∈[M],n∈[Nm]}\{(x_{m},y_{m}^{(n)}):m\in[M],n\in[N_{m}]\} [74, 62, 59, 47]:

1M​∑m=1M1Nm​∑n=1Nmwm(n)​ri​(xm,ym(n))​ where ​wm(n)=π⁡(ym(n)|xm)/π0​(ym(n)|xm)∑n′=1Nmπ⁡(ym(n′)|xm)/π0​(ym(n′)|xm)\displaystyle\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\frac{1}{N_{m}}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{m}}w_{m}^{(n)}r_{i}(x_{m},y_{m}^{(n)})\text{\quad where \quad}w_{m}^{(n)}=\frac{\pi(y_{m}^{(n)}|x_{m})/\pi_{0}(y_{m}^{(n)}|x_{m})}{\sum_{n^{\prime}=1}^{N_{m}}\pi(y_{m}^{(n^{\prime})}|x_{m})/\pi_{0}(y_{m}^{(n^{\prime})}|x_{m})}

After training all the models described above, we use weighted importance sampling to estimate the expected rewards of every checkpoint from {20%, 30%, 40%, 50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 90%, 100%} of their respective training trajectories. We then identify the resulting Pareto fronts of these expected rewards across all preference vectors used and report their hypervolumes in Table 1. We also visualize these Pareto fronts and present a more qualitative analysis in Appendix A.

STOMP’s expected rewards achieve the best hypervolume in 8 of the 9 evaluation settings. In the ninth (α-amylase with RA-10B), STOMP is second-best and achieves 98.7% of the performance of the best method. STOMP also outperforms the next-best algorithm by >10% relative in 3 settings (PbrR with PG3, PbrR with RA-3B and α-amylase with PG3). Meanwhile, there are no consistent winners between the three baseline algorithms across the different datasets and base models. Thus, STOMP demonstrates the best ability to cover the full Pareto front of the methods tested while being highly robust to the underlying dataset and base model being used.

4.4 Evaluating Generated Proteins

For each (dataset, base model, algorithm) combination, we select the two checkpoints whose offline expected rewards achieve the greatest hypervolumes (one checkpoint if it is the only point on the Pareto front), and we generate novel sequences from these checkpoints. We then use Gaussian process reward models to estimate the expected rewards of these generated sequences and compute the expected hypervolumes (along with their uncertainties) achieved by random samples of k∈{12,24,48,96,192,384}k\in\{12,24,48,96,192,384\} generated sequences. These represent realistic sample sizes that one might test in a small wet lab experiment. See Appendix C for more details.

For the DHFR dataset, we select the four DHFR homologs from the training set that maximize the hypervolume. We prompt PG3 with the first 20 residues (out of 161–170 total) on either the N- or C-terminal. For the RA models, we also prepend the prompts used for training. For all models, we autoregressively generate 100,000 proteins via top-pp sampling with p=0.95p=0.95 and temperatures τ∈[0.5,1.0]\tau\in[0.5,1.0] [33], and we apply the quality filtering criteria of Bhatnagar et al. [7].

While all methods achieve similar hypervolumes in the offline evaluation for the DHFR dataset (Table 1), clear performance gaps emerge when we evaluate their generations (Figure 3, Row 1). This discrepancy stems from a limitation of the offline evaluation: the DHFR dataset comprises highly diverse homologs that the models can easily distinguish, and all methods consistently assign high likelihood to the test sequences that achieve high hypervolumes. However, for the more challenging generation task, RA-3B (Row 1, Column 2) and RA-10B (Row 1, Column 3) aligned with STOMP generate sequences with the best predicted activity, especially when working with small sample sizes. For PG3 (Row 1, Column 1), all methods perform similarly.

In contrast to the DHFR dataset of diverse homologs, the PbrR and α-amylase datasets are local mutational landscapes of a single wild-type protein. Any reward model trained on this dataset would therefore be less reliable at predicting the quality of diverse generations from an autoregressive PLM. We instead use the Gibbs with Gradient (GWG) algorithm to propose mutations to the wild type protein using PLM negative log likelihoods as an energy function [30]. Because GWG is a Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, we can use the sequences sampled from it to estimate the expected rewards of sampling from the PLM of interest while remaining in-distribution for our reward models [59, 30]. For each model, we run 1500 GWG trajectories for 300 steps each and filter out any sequences with >10 mutations, since these are likely out-of-distribution for our reward models. For the RA models, these trajectories are evenly split across the different training prompts.

For PbrR (Figure 2, Row 2), STOMP achieves the highest expected hypervolume for all base models (often in a tie), with second place varying between base models. Results are more challenging to interpret for α-amylase (Figure 2, Row 3), since all methods perform quite similarly both to each other and to the unaligned pretrained model. It is unclear whether this is because alignment on this dataset is challenging, or because the Gaussian process reward models are unable to detect differences between the generated proteins.

Interestingly, ODPO-STZ’s performance across different evaluation settings is highly inconsistent. It obtains the second-highest expected hypervolumes for DHFR with RA-10B and PbrR with PG3 (Figure 2, (Row 1, Column 3), (Row 2, Column 1)), but the worst expected hypervolumes (besides the pretrained model) for DHFR with RA-3B and PbrR with both RA models (Figure 2, (Row 1, Column 2), (Row 2, Column 2), (Row 2, Column 3)). This variability highlights the importance of our principled derivation in Section 3.1 in elucidating the appropriate techniques to apply smooth Tchebysheff scalarization to offline multi-objective RL.

5 Discussion

In multi-objective reinforcment learning (RL), a fundamental limitation of linear reward scalarization is its inability to recover the full Pareto front of optimal solutions. This paper introduces Smooth Tchebysheff Optimization of Multi-Objective Preferences (STOMP), a novel offline multi-objective RL algorithm. Rather than taking the standard approach of directly scalarizing the reward, we instead derive STOMP by framing multi-objective RL itself as the optimization problem to be scalarized using smooth Tchebysheff scalarization, a recently proposed technique that overcomes the shortcomings of linear scalarization.

Our experiments across multiple protein language models and biological datasets demonstrate that STOMP consistently outperforms existing baselines, achieving superior coverage of the Pareto front in both offline off-policy and generative evaluations. We thus show that STOMP is well-poised to improve a broad range of multi-objective protein optimization workflows. However, the method itself is domain-agnostic and can be used for any multi-objective alignment application, including the post-training of chatbots or text-to-image generators.

More broadly, the smooth Tchebysheff reward scalarziations derived from Optimization Problems 6–7 are completely general to any KL-constrained or maximum-entropy RL formulation. A natural extension of our work would be applying these scalarizations to multi-objective online RL. A key challenge to overcome in this setting would be estimating the partition functions Zi​(x)Z_{i}(x) when sequences yy are not collated in an offline dataset but are instead generated in an online fashion.

Finally, in Section 3.1, we leveraged the framing of maximum-entropy RL to scalarize the rewards RSTλ,πR_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda,\pi} and RSTλR_{\text{ST}}^{\lambda} (Equations 8–9), since the reward represents a ground truth that should not depend on a potentially sub-optimal reference policy π0\pi_{0}. However, STOMP implicitly constrains the KL divergence between the learned policy π\pi and a pre-trained or fine-tuned π0\pi_{0}. This is because our early experiments found that maximum-entropy variants of STOMP (i.e. removing the log⁡π0​(y|x)\log\pi_{0}(y|x) terms from Equation 11) suffered from training instability and sensitivity to hyperparameters. We leave further study of such reference-free losses to future work.
